extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy; translators and scholars of Schopenhauer
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reading, translating, and understanding Arthur Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation, including epistemological, aesthetic, ontological, and ethical theses and how to approach the work. Useful for readers, translators, and scholars seeking interpretive or practical criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite reading / assumed background
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer demands that his doctoral dissertation On the Fourfold Root of the Principle of Sufficient Reason be read before WWR and that the reader be familiar with Kant's philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer states it is 'absolutely impossible to truly understand the present work unless the reader is familiar with this introduction' and that the contents of that essay are presupposed 'as much as if they had been included in the book.' He also says the book 'assumes the reader's prior knowledge of the philosophy of Immanuel Kant.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended reading approach: study repeatedly and patiently
rubrics_metrics.description: The work's structure is 'organic rather than chainlike' and its parts are 'bound together most intimately,' requiring multiple readings for full comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer counsels reading the book more than once with considerable patience the first time; only repeated study will clarify how the parts 'reciprocally illuminate each other' and make the single thought clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation choice for Vorstellung (representation/idea/presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translators must choose how to render the key term Vorstellung, with important interpretive consequences (options used historically: 'idea', 'representation', 'presentation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Haldane & Kemp used 'idea'; Payne and Norman/Welchman/Janaway use 'representation'; Aquila argues for 'presentation' to emphasize the performative/presentational activity of the subject. The choice affects how readers understand the dual notion of what is 'set before' a subject and the presentational activity of the subject itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the work as an exposition of a single, unified thought
rubrics_metrics.description: WWR aims to 'convey a single thought' developed from four complementary perspectives (epistemology, ontology, aesthetics, ethics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the book unfolds one thought across four books, each part presupposes others; readers should treat the work as an organic unity rather than a sequence of independent essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemological framing: world as representation under the principle of sufficient reason
rubrics_metrics.description: In Book I Schopenhauer considers the world as representation — objects ordered by space, time and cause-and-effect — and subject to the principle of sufficient reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should evaluate claims about knowledge and phenomena within the framework that our experience is representation (Vorstellung) ordered by the principle of sufficient reason; Book III later treats representation independent of that principle (Platonic Idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontological claim: the will as the thing-in-itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer identifies the thing-in-itself (Kantian noumenon) with will — a blind, unconscious, aimless striving outside space and time and free of multiplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To accept Schopenhauer's metaphysics is to accept that the inner essence of everything is will and that plurality appears only through time and space (principium individuationis); this is foundational for his arguments in later books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection / simplification of Kantian categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer rejects most of Kant's twelve categories as superfluous and reduces the a priori forms that render experience intelligible to three: time, space, and causality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations of WWR should account for Schopenhauer's claim that eleven of Kant's categories are 'blind windows' and that time, space and causality suffice for the ordering of experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic criterion: pure, will-less contemplation (Platonic Idea knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetic contemplation consists in knowing an object not as an individual but as a universal Platonic Idea, enabling a temporary escape from the will as a 'pure, will-less subject of knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art (works that elucidate the visibility of the will) is valued insofar as it facilitates objective, will-less contemplation; Schopenhauer treats art as a 'camera obscura' showing objects more purely. This is the standard for judging works as beautiful or sublime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for beauty and the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects are beautiful if they best facilitate pure, objective contemplation and express 'elevated' Ideas (e.g., humanity). The sublime involves struggling over hostility to the object and being elevated above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments of beauty should focus on how an object allows the subject to become will-less and apprehend universal Ideas; the sublime is marked by a different affective response—elevation through struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns in art: stimulation of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Works that stimulate the will (e.g., depictions of nude women or appetizing food) hinder aesthetic contemplation and so are criticized by Schopenhauer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating art according to Schopenhauer, consider whether the object stimulates desire (serving the will) versus facilitating disinterested contemplation; stimulating desire counts against aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as a criterion for artistic production and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is the capacity for aesthetic experience present in varying degrees in people; those with high genius can be taught to communicate aesthetic experiences to others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of artistic creation should take into account the artist's capacity to access and convey the universal Ideas that produce disinterested contemplation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music's privileged status in aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Music is an immediate objectification and copy of the whole will itself (not merely of the Ideas) and thus is more powerful and penetrating than other arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In comparative aesthetic evaluation, Schopenhauer ranks music above other arts because it directly expresses the will; its effect is 'much more powerful' since it copies the essence rather than the shadow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical criterion: affirmation vs denial of the will; compassion as transcendence
rubrics_metrics.description: Human ethical behavior consists in affirmation or denial of the 'will to life.' Compassion arises from transcending egoism (recognizing illusory individuality) and can point toward negating desire and the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral worth in Schopenhauer's scheme is tied to the degree to which actions manifest compassion (transcendence of egoistic will) or participate in ascetic denial; violent acts like suicide are relativized (they do not destroy the will), whereas ascetic practices gradually weaken individual will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asceticism as the path to salvation
rubrics_metrics.description: True redemption from suffering can only result from the ascetic, total negation of the will to life; asceticism is superior to suicide as a means of weakening the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of religious or ethical practices should consider their relation to negating the will: Eastern monastic asceticism and certain saints are praised, while other religious forms are criticized for optimism or cruelty to animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative/supplementary reading: payoff from familiarity with Plato and the Upanishads
rubrics_metrics.description: Schopenhauer states that prior familiarity with Plato and the Upanishads will place the reader at an advantage in understanding his theories, especially regarding aesthetics and salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers and interpreters may benefit from consulting Platonic and Upanishadic texts to grasp Schopenhauer's appeals to Platonic Ideas and Indian metaphysical concepts (e.g., Tat Tvam Asi).
